Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
May I invite you to state your full name, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: My name is Dr Emma Jane Lewis.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Dr Lewis, could you tell us something of your occupation? We are particularly interested in your occupation as of 2016.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: 2016. I'm a consultant clinical biochemist. I work within the blood sciences laboratories at the Countess of Chester Hospital. I was doing that in 2016 and I'm still there now.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Could you, in a sentence or two, describe the role of a consultant clinical scientist within the laboratories at the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So my role -- a lot of that is to provide advice about test results, about how samples are collected, if there are any
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: special procedures required, to give advice to consultants, to anybody who basically asks for advice from us, and also I'm concerned with the overall running of the department as well.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. Do your responsibilities extend to ensuring the protocols and the integrity of the laboratory to ensure the quality of results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. We would put in place procedures so that the quality of the results that we produce would be accurate.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm now going to continue to ask you some questions of general application before we move to a specific set of tests and results.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The general topic is blood testing. How is a request for a blood test generated within the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So in 2016, you could have either requested a test or a series of tests within our electronic patient record or you could have used a paper-based request form; either were acceptable at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Let's concentrate on the former for a moment. How would the user, how would the doctor or the nurse who wished for a test to be undertaken, how would they make the request through the computerised system?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Through the computerised system there was a requesting panel, so you could request laboratory tests within this, within this module, within the hospital system.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: All the tests that we do within the laboratory were on that system and it was just a case of finding which test you want, clicking on "add", and requesting those on the system, and that would form the basis of that request.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: So that would be a medic or a nurse --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: -- making the request on a desktop computer --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: -- within their unit --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: -- for example? Such a request having been made, how would it be received within the laboratory?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So once the sample had been collected, the sample can either be sent via -- we have a pod system within the hospital, so basically you just put the sample and the request form in a tube, put it through the pod system, and it arrives in the lab. Or it can be transported by hand, either by somebody from the ward or a porter can do that as well, to come to the laboratory.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: The request for a test having been made within the unit, and we here, of course, are focusing upon the neonatal unit, that request having been made, would the fact of a request having been made be communicated to the laboratory before the sample was podded and sent in?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The requests were on the system but they weren't actually downloaded into the pathology part of that module until we actually received that request within the laboratory. And then we physically had to download the data from our -- not download the data, but receive it, and it wouldn't actually come into our part of the module until we received the sample.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: But the making of the request, would that be logged within the system?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That was logged within the system, yes. Once the request has been made, it is on the system.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: And the logging of the making of the request, what information would be contained within that log?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So on that information, you would have details of the person who requested it, you would have the time that it was requested, you would have all the information that the laboratory required, so all the patient information, so their name, date of birth, things like that. And you would have the list of tests that were required within that request.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Sorry to be pedantic, but you said the time of the request would be logged and, I assume, the date?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And the date, yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: That having been made within, for example, the neonatal unit, what, if anything, would be generated at that end within the unit at that point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe at the time you could have generated -- you were generating a paper-based request form at the time.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's move then to the point in time where a blood sample, for example, has been taken from a patient.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: What would be the next stage in the procedure within the unit as far as you are aware?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As far as I am aware, once a blood sample has been taken, it would then be sent to the laboratory. As I said, either by the podding system or by somebody physically taking it to the laboratory.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Let's consider what it is that's being podded or handdelivered to the laboratory. Blood?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Where would that be stored?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The blood is in a tube. And obviously seeing it's a neonatal tube, it would be in what we call a paediatric size tube. These are very small tubes, they only take about -- 1.3ml, I think, is the size of blood they take. From a neonatal unit we generally don't get full tubes of blood.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. What, if anything, would be labelled or marked on that tube to identify the patient, the substance and the testing request?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the tubes we'd get from the neonatal unit generally have what we call a patient identification sticker wrapped round. The tubes are generally far too small to actually write on. There's a label you can write on but they are very small so what they generally do is put a patient identification label on the tubes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Are you aware of how the patient identification label is generated?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Um... I have to say I'm not 100% on how these things are generated.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. So let's move to the point in time where the sample is received by the laboratory. At that point in time, is the laboratory forewarned or notified of the arrival of a sample?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Generally not unless we have to do something with it particularly quickly or it needs to be -- or it needs special attention or anything. Generally, the samples just arrive within the laboratory.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: How do your colleagues at the laboratory know what is requested of them?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because they will have the request form and they will also be able to look on the computer system and that request will be on the system with the details of everything that is required.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll come to a specific example in due course, but at the moment staying with general matters, could I ask you now about the testing process.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: We are primarily here concerned with a blood sample and most specifically for tests for insulin and C-peptide levels, as I know you're aware. What is the testing process within the laboratory for blood samples to achieve that end?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: For blood samples, depending on the type of testing, there would either be put straight on an analyser or, if we don't need the cellular component of the blood, they would be centrifuged before being sent to the analysers. With adult tubes we have automation within the laboratory, so the centrifugation is a completely automated system, but with paediatric samples they are treated manually because they are so small and they are manually centrifuged and then anything -- the serum at the top of the sample, which is the bit that we use, is manually taken off and put into a different tube so that that can then go on the analyser.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Could you kindly explain the process of manual centrifugation in words that I can understand?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. So we have the tube, we have what we call desktop size centrifuges, so these are centrifuges that are probably about that sort of size (indicating). They have special inserts in them that can take these very small paediatric tubes that we have. We put them in the centrifuge, they're spun, basically like a washing machine spinning, for a fixed amount of time at a fixed rate. Once they're done, they're taken out and if you hold them up, you can see a clear separation between the cellular material that will be at the bottom of the tube and the bit that we want to test, which is the sort of straw-like serum or plasma at the top of the tube.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: So this spinning process separates these two components --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: -- of the blood and allows you to isolate the part that you're most interested in --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: -- the serum?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: What happens next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If it's a paediatric sample, we don't put those tubes directly on to the analyser, we take off the serum or the plasma at the top of the tube, we put it into what we call a micro cup. These are little tubes, little cups that can go into separate tubes so they can be put on the analyser to be sampled and to be tested.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: We, as you know, are interested in insulin C-peptide tests. The sample having been spun, the components having been separated, would that test be undertaken within your laboratory at Chester?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We don't analyse insulin and C-peptide levels, we send them away to be tested, we send them to the Royal Liverpool Hospital.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Could you help us understand the process between the spinning, the separation and the sample being delivered to the Royal Liverpool Hospital?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The sample would have been separated as I have detailed in the centrifuge, the plasma would have been taken off, it would have been put into a separate tube, a slightly bigger tube, not a micro tube that we use for the analysers. It would have been labelled with all the patient identification. And because it's for insulin and C-peptide, it actually would have been frozen at that point because insulin is (inaudible) unstable.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Could you assist us as to the transport process?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So we have a hospital transport that goes every day from the laboratory and takes any samples that we need to send to Liverpool directly to their laboratories over there.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. We've heard from your colleagues at the Royal Liverpool Hospital as to the testing process within there. Could you tell us, from your perspective, about the receipt of results from Liverpool?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So we get results back from Liverpool, normally in paper -- on paper. We would get a paper copy of the report. If the result is very abnormal or there is something that somebody needs to do something about relatively quickly we may get a phone call from them saying, "We have this result for you".
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: You may receive a phone call if the results are abnormal, am I right to assume, because through that method the information is communicated to you more quickly?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: If that isn't done, what's the usual time lag between sending to Liverpool and receiving the paper results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It very much depends on the test being done, how often Liverpool do the test, whether it's something they would do daily or maybe it's something they would do weekly.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: It's very variable as to how fast we get these results back.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: In circumstances where you receive results orally through a telephone call, how is the fact of that communication and the content of that communication recorded within your laboratory?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It may well be -- if we get a result that's phoned to us we will put it on the computer system and some people when they put these results in will say -- will put a note in to say it's been communicated from the referring hospital, but it's not a sort of written down procedure as, it were, that we have to do that. So sometimes people will just put the results on the system.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask you to assist us understand a document that's been generated by your system and has been exhibited by you as part of your statement-making process.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: If I could ask Mr Murphy to take us to tile 190.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There's a screen to your right. Dr Lewis, and members of the jury, there's a paper copy of this behind our divider 16, I think. Yes. Of [Baby L]. It's a document that we looked at briefly the other day, it has EL/3 at the top.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Click behind there, please, Mr Murphy. Dr Lewis, there's a mouse by your right hand. If that assists you to take us to relevant parts, I encourage you to do so.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Divider 15, members of the jury, not 16. 16 is [Baby M], 15 is [Baby L].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recognise this document?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So you've got a run date here, so that's the time and the date that this was printed. And this is the user here, so that's my mnemonic(?) there.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. The remainder of this document, is this information and data that was put on the system back in 2016?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. This is information about the patient and also some audit data about times when various things happened to that sample.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. So let's look at it -- we've got the patient's name, which we're familiar with. We have details about his age and date of birth in the next part of this band of information. Does the remainder simply seek to inform you where he was at the time the sample was taken?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: And the location?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: What about the far right of this band? What does that tell you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This bit here (indicating)?
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the CC here is his hospital number. This is a registration date. And this is his discharge date.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Obviously, this was produced well after he was discharged so it actually has a discharge on it, but sometimes that wouldn't be filled in.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: So the CC is [Baby L]'s unique patient reference number?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: We understand the discharge date, I'm sure. But what about the middle entry, the reg?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm assuming -- I'm not entirely sure, I assume it's some sort of registration date.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Registration of what, do you know?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Probably the patient because it's --
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Well, it was his birth date. The day he came into the world.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's move to the next section.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Moving from left to right, thank you, Mr Murphy. SPEC to the left?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This one here (indicating)?
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This is a laboratory -- this is part of the way we record -- it's a laboratory number.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. Is that a reference to the sample, to the test?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's the sample number.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: That's the sample reference, thank you. Let's move to the next three entries. Just to the right of the same -- so ORDER, FOR, COL and RECV.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Order, that's the date it was ordered. Collected, that is an automatic infill because we don't actually -- there was no recording of when the sample was actually collected --
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- but that's the date it was received in the laboratory, the date and time it was received within the laboratory system.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Right. Pausing there, so the system, the laboratory, was not provided with a time for the taking of the sample; is that the position?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: And does UNK mean unknown?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: But you do have a time and date stamp for the receipt of it --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: -- the sample, into the laboratory?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. We see on the next column, status, consultant/GP, and we have the name we're familiar with and that's a doctor who's already given evidence before this jury.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The final entry, REQ?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So this is a request number, but this is something that we don't particularly use in the laboratory, but it's an audit function within the entire hospital system.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: So that's the audit reference for the request to undertake the test?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe that is, yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving back to the left of the page, we've got four sets of digits.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Order number, could you decode that for us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: These are the individual order numbers for some of the individual tests. Some of the -- for the tests that are requested here, they're going to different analysers so they actually require different individual sort of order numbers or request numbers to go to the different analysers. There are four there because there are, I think, four different types of test there.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. Next, beneath -- we'll go line by line from left to right. We see entered and then we have the date again, 9 April 2016 and the time. Staying with the time for a moment, 15.45, what does that inform the reader?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe that that is the time that the request was actually made.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: So the request from the NNU --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: -- to the laboratory?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: If we just remind ourselves, for tests of a sample that was received at -- on 9 April 2016 and it looks like at 18.26.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Again, that request at 15.45, if we go from left to right, was made by Dr Ukoh?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. This is collected by -- this is the mnemonic of one of our biomedical scientists within the lab.

blocks.text: Although it has to be said because the collection module in the system didn't actually work, that mnemonic is actually the person who received the sample within the laboratory.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I think that's last reported. Yes, that's the last time that the result was actually looked at within the system.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: And that's 19 October 2018, so way beyond --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: -- the time we're very concerned with?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: An action.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: But that action could be an administrative action as opposed to a scientific testing action?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Next line, "ordered"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This the mnemonic for the series of tests that were ordered on this baby. So U&E is a urea and electrolytes, we have insulin and C-peptide, we have a cortisol and we have growth hormone.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Comments?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the comments is just any clinical comments or any clinical information that is made by the doctor at the time of the request. So you can see here the clinical details they've put in were "hypoglycaemia neonate".
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: So that's a reference to the baby who's providing the sample?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Just going to the right:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She is Dr Shirley Bowles, she is our consultant chemical pathologist.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So what happens -- not all tests go through the system automatically, some are held back for review by whoever is acting as duty biochemist that day. So the cortisol and the growth hormone would have been on a fertility sheet. That's a set of tests that require a view before they are put on the system for review by either consultants, doctors or whoever's requested them.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving down, we see "perform site". Could you help us understand that and the entry beneath it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So this is the lab, so it has been -- testing has been performed within the laboratory on that time and date.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: So that was when the testing of the sample was started.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving along that line, "at site", we see to the right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again, I think that's just laboratory, it was performed at our site rather than anywhere else.

blocks.text: Beneath that is "report audit"; is that of any significance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, that just tells us where and when data has been sent. The second one, obviously a copy of results was sent out to ward 36, which is this one here, at that time and date.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. So that records or creates an audit trail for the communication of the results --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: -- once the process has been completed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: So that would tend to suggest that ward 36 was informed of the results at 12.47 on 14 April?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think -- yes, that date there is the completion date, so the date when everything was complete.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Thank you. If Mr Murphy scrolls down so we can see entries 1 to 9. Here we have a bank of similar looking entries. Generally speaking, what are they?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's audit information as to when results were available -- were sent out from the system from the pathology laboratory system on to the hospital system and what time they would have been viewable by people on the ward. So you've got the time and date there.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: "Result out" just means that results are going out.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: This Iguana here, this is just the name of the integration engine, so it's part of the system that sends results out from the pathology module to the main hospital system. I'm not sure what this record number here is. This is sent and this is the user who was involved.
blocks.speaker: LEWIS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
