blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You've told us the basis for your instructions. So far as the material that you were sent, were you sent, in short form, [Baby L]'s medical records from the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The blood test results that were available for [Baby L] covering this period of time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I received those as well.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And did you also receive, in addition to Dr Evans' report, a report from or reports from Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you. Were you told that it was suspected that [Baby L] had either been given an injection or infusion of insulin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And were you told that the reasoning behind the suspicion was that there was a mismatch between the level of Cpeptide and insulin in a blood sample?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So, so far as the specific questions that you were asked to address, were they as follows? First, what had caused the high insulin and low C-peptide level?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Were you asked whether you agreed with the conclusions of Doctors Evans and Bohin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: If you did agree, were you asked why you agreed with them?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Alternatively, if you did not agree, were you asked to say why?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was asked that question.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And in that event to explain what you thought had happened?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Were you asked specifically to address the issue of naturally occurring conditions that an infant could suffer that would leave a high insulin level and low C-peptide concurrently?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And were you asked to help with how those conditions could be identified?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: If there were other potential causes for the findings, what evidence there was for and against that particular proposition in this particular case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that was included in the request.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you. And finally, were you asked to say how common it was to find such a disparity between insulin and Cpeptide?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And/or any other conditions that you identified that could account for the readings?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you. So far as [Baby L]'s background is concerned, did you summarise his arrival in the world and treatment at the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And did you set out at least a good proportion of the readings that are now reproduced in this table that we've spent some time going through?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is correct, and I've certainly documented right up to 16.00 hours and then I took up the values again on the measurement at 22.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I'm looking at, in my version of your report, page 4.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't know if it corresponds precisely with the printed copy that you have. But did you refer specifically to the document that the witness this morning was being asked about, which is the printout from the lab? I think if you go to jury bundle 2, it's page 18026.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm on that page, yes. I recognise the data output and the values recorded as the ones that I used in the formation of this report.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you. So you were looking at the glucose reading, cortisol, growth hormone, insulin, C-peptide, sodium and potassium?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: What struck you as being unusual, if anything, about these results?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So in the face of the plasma glucose value, we have a plasma insulin concentration of 1,099 picomoles per litre, and insulin C-peptide of 264 picomoles per litre, plus a cortisol of 397 millimoles per litre, which is raised, and blood plasma growth hormone of 8.63 micrograms per litre, also elevated.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The elevation of the plasma cortisol and plasma growth hormone largely excludes ketotic hypoglycaemia as a cause.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. This is highly technical for people like me. So you started by looking at cortisol and growth hormone?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. They were both elevated, as you would expect in a situation where you are hypoglycaemic. So the responses, although elevated, are correct and appropriate for the hypoglycaemia.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Why does that exclude what you've just told us?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because they are one of the -- deficiencies of cortisol and growth hormone are one of the major causes for ketotic hypoglycaemia.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So that is a form of hypoglycaemia?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And that can be -- deficiencies there can be a cause?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: But not here?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But not here because we're going to come on to considering the other form of hypoglycaemia, which is nonketotic hypoglycaemia.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You have just mentioned ketotic hypoglycaemia.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is this one of the naturally occurring potential causes of low blood sugar?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So two hormones measured, those results in your opinion excluded the possibility of this particular type of naturally occurring low blood sugar?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So turning to non-ketotic hypoglycaemia?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Non-ketotic hypoglycaemia is driven by two large causes: one is excess of insulin and the other is a deficiency in the formation of acylcarnitine, which I think we can exclude because we have here clearly documented high plasma insulin concentrations, which you do not get in non-ketotic hypoglycaemia due to acylcarnitine problems.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Acylcarnitine problems. Problems is a word I know.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can you explain the rest of it, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In order to form ketone bodies when you're starving, you have to break down fat in the liver and the process that does that operates or uses the carnitine system to promote the breakdown of your stored fat into ketone bodies, which the brain
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: can use as an alternative source of energy when glucose is not available.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: You described this to us last time, didn't you, in [Baby F]'s case, when you were telling us how dangerous it is to have an overdose of insulin because the overdose of insulin prevents the body's backup or plan B, which is when, as you say, you're starving, you consume fat, and the fat in effect keeps the brain functioning?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is absolutely correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Right, I'm glad I understood that. All right. So we have two potential causes for high insulin, which you have excluded for those reasons; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I've excluded one cause for non-ketotic hypoglycaemia, which is this acylcarnitine side of things.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I am now left with a situation of hypoglycaemia associated with an elevated plasma insulin concentration, and the question then is: is the source of that insulin from the body itself endogenous insulin or is it from somewhere else, from outside the body, exogenous insulin? And to direct us to which of the two it might be, we have an associated measurement of the plasma C-peptide concentration, and because of the way that insulin and C-peptide are produced and removed from the circulation, the concentration of C-peptide is always five to ten times the concentration of insulin.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So if your plasma insulin was 10 picomoles per litre you'd expect your C-peptide going with that measurement to be somewhere in the region of between 50 and 100 picomoles per litre.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So always a situation where the insulin is coming from the pancreas of the individual, when you measure insulin and Cpeptide together, the C-peptide will always be greater than the insulin. This is not the case looking at these particular measurements. You can see that the plasma insulin is high at 1,099 picomoles per litre. If we were to apply our rule of it being five to ten times -- of the C-peptide being five to ten times the plasma insulin concentration, we should see a plasma C-peptide concentration of somewhere between 5,000 to 10,000 picomoles per litre.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: We do not see that. What we see is a plasma C-peptide which is down towards the bottom end of the range quoted by the laboratory. It's on the basis of that that I concluded the view
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: of the two paediatricians who reviewed this case was correct in that the cause for the hypoglycaemia was the exogenous administration of insulin.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you. So somebody gave insulin to [Baby L]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And I think we should -- yes, I agree with that statement. I think we should add, to qualify it perhaps, also, that this was not prescribed insulin.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: No. Would it also be -- plainly, there is no prescription in the medical records, but would any of these blood glucose readings justify somebody giving insulin to this child?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: On the data that we are presented with in the table from this morning, there is no indication whatsoever for the administration of insulin. The only occasion when that would take place would be if there was persistent raised blood glucose values. This is not the case at all in the recordings that we have observed over the period of time from 9 April through to 11 April.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: You told us last time of the dangers of administering insulin in a case where it is not medically indicated.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do they apply equally to this particular case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They are exactly the same.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you. You told us last time that you can't give insulin orally because, basically, it won't -- for the reasons you explained about the size, it's a protein, the size of the molecule and all the rest of it, it doesn't pass through the system through the stomach?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Therefore, given the range and duration of the low blood sugar readings, by what means was, in your opinion, insulin given to [Baby L]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think the most likely way of administering it would be by the intravenous route. The other route you could administer the insulin is by injection under the skin.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: But assuming that the insulin used was Actrapid insulin, ultrashort-acting insulin, which is available as ward stock, the duration of action would require, over the time period we are discussing, some seven to eight subcutaneous injections in order to maintain this period of hypoglycaemia.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: If the route was intravenous we have two options.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: One is to give multiple single -- sorry, multiple injections, intravenous bolus injections of insulin.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Again, the duration of action would dictate that you would need to give somewhere between 10 and 12, perhaps 14, single intravenous bolus injections to achieve the same effect in terms of blood glucose over this period.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: If you went for an infusion of insulin intravenously, then that would require adding insulin to the infusion system, the bags that have been used to deliver fluid, and depending on how often the bags are changed, you would not need to alter -- you would not need to have such a frequent attention to administering the insulin, you could make up several bags at once, for example, perhaps, and that would be sufficient to cover this time period.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So my feeling is that the likely mode of delivery of the insulin was through an intravenous infusion by the addition of exogenous insulin to the infusion bag systems.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The next question which you address in your written report is how much needs to go into the bag to produce these figures.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, the answer is that I've taken quite a conservative view of this and I would suggest that you could add somewhere in the region of 10 units of insulin to a bag and that would be sufficient to produce the hypoglycaemic effect and also to generate the plasma insulin concentration that was measured in the sample on 9 April.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: For your information, the vials of insulin contain 100 units per millilitre, so 10 units is a tenth of a millilitre. So the volumes we're talking about are quite small and would not be noticeable just on a routine stock check. If added to infusion bags, you wouldn't notice the change in the volume within the bag, nor, because insulin is -- Actrapid insulin, I should say, is a clear solution, would you see any change in the colouration of the fluid in the bag, nor would you see any cloudiness in the bag itself, which you might see in some of the older insulins that we used many years ago.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: One issue that's been raised with a number of witnesses is that insulin has a distinctive smell. Would you smell it in the bag?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it has a distinctive smell, but you wouldn't smell it. You would only really smell insulin if you're drawing
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: it up and you get it on your hands. But otherwise, no, once it's in the bag, it's in a sense sealed off from you being able to detect it by smell.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Just going back over to some of that information that you've given to us, 10 units equals one tenth of 1 millilitre; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The jury saw, and you produced last time, a little vial of Actrapid insulin, which is the type of insulin that there was on the ward at the time. That's a 10ml bottle; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So as a 10ml bottle, just to give us some idea of what we're talking about, that bottle contains 1,000 units?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So it's 1% of that 10ml bottle, putting it in another way?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: How does one get insulin if one were determined to do it? How would you get it into a bag of dextrose?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You can do it fairly easily: you would draw it up with a needle and syringe, and on the infusion bags you can inject it either -- through the portal is the easiest way to do it. You could just push it into the bag itself, but you're always susceptible then to it leaking if it just went straight into the bag rather than through the portal at the bottom of the bag.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: It may be outside your personal experience, I don't know, but we've seen videos or a video of a nurse increasing the volume of dextrose in a bag or the concentration of dextrose and going through a specifically designed port, which, if the bag was hanging, would be at the bottom of the bag.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That would be the most likely way of doing it.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you. The next question, professor, is, if possible, can you help the jury with how many bags were contaminated? The jury will have to draw their own conclusions, but if the exogenous insulin was first administered some time on 9 April, we see a very low reading of blood sugar at 10 am, 10.00 hours. We know that 10% insulin, so whether it was one or
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: two bags of that were in use between -- I keep making this mistake, I'm sorry, I do it in writing as well, I say insulin instead of dextrose, I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: 10% dextrose. I'll start again. What we see on the 9th is 10% dextrose running in effect all day --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Despite -- the overwhelming, almost inevitable, I would suggest, inference is that the blood sample that was taken and analysed in the lab was taken before that change, all right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So it would follow from that, would it, that there must have been insulin in that 10% bag?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So we've got insulin in one bag, which is the 10% bag, running up to about 16.30. Of course we have no blood sample taken after 16.30 on the 9th, but we have a continuing low blood glucose despite that infusion.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So looking at the rate, if there was no insulin being administered to [Baby L] during the period from 16.30 onwards, given the amount of dextrose he was receiving, would you expect the dextrose to have raised his blood sugar above those figures that we see for the balance of 9 April, continuing into the 10th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, for two reasons, both of which are rather similar.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The first thing is that, if I may go back to the glucose delivery, the glucose delivery from that change at 16.30 hours is to a glucose delivery rate of 8.4 milligrams per kilogram body weight per minute. So we're above our value of 5 milligrams per kilogram per minute, so above what you would normally expect to maintain a normal blood glucose, and I would expect the glucose concentrations to rise as a result of that.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So 5 is the requirement?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And there's 8.4 being delivered without any feed or any other -- just from the bag?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So in percentage terms, that's, what, 68% extra?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The situation changes further if we go down to 22.00 hours where there's a further step up in the infusion rate and that then now delivers 12.7 milligrams per kilogram body weight per minute. So more than double your --
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: It's 140% extra --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: -- give or take?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So do you infer from that or those data that this child must have been receiving insulin during that period as well?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. That would be taken as evidence for ongoing insulin action and it must be continuous insulin action -- or continued, I should say.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes. Does that continue through the following day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Essentially, it does. You can see some variations in the infusion rate, but whatever way you look at it, it is more than a 5 milligrams per kilogram body weight per minute infusion rate, even when we get down to 5ml per hour. For example, at 04.00 hours on 10 April, we are only down to 8.5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per minute. So we've still got quite a high glucose requirement during this period of time.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: All right. So you have helpfully there picked a time after which the concentration of the bag had increased again?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So we're on to a third bag by this stage. So in terms of how -- what are the possibilities in terms of how, if bags were being changed, despite that fact, insulin is continuing to be administered to [Baby L]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I suppose my first question back to you is: are the bags changed? And secondly -- well, let's deal with that first.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The evidence suggests that the bags are changed.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I don't think that's a controversial statement. It's a matter for the jury whether they were or they weren't, but the system, as it's been relayed to us, is that the standard stock back is a 10% bag. To make it up 12% or 15% they add 50% at a given ratio to produce the required concentration.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So that's the evidence.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Into a new bag?
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Into a new bag.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And do we also take it as a given that when they're doing that procedure, the whole giving system is changed as well?
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We don't know?
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: It's just a change of the bag. Well, it's for the jury to decide.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There have been different things said about the giving sets on this particular charge.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: On this one.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's a tricky one now. Can I just take that as the bags are changed and we'll leave the giving set out of it? Then we have a 10% bag, we have a 12.5% bag made up, we have a 15% bag made up, and those three, depending on when they are run out and changed again -- so we're probably talking about a minimum of three bags having insulin added to them potentially.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: If the giving set isn't changed, what other possibilities enter the considerations?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The giving sets are plastic and insulin is a protein and it sticks very nicely to plastic. So in your giving set as
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: well you would have insulin stuck potentially on to the walls of the tubing from which it could fall off over a period of time as well.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes. So even if you run insulin through a giving set from a bag, you replace the bag but don't put insulin into the new bag, you will still have insulin passing in the fluid --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: -- to the child?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I suppose another alternative is -- well, someone can put insulin into each bag. That's one possibility?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, perfectly possible.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: As I have already told you, there is some uncertainty as to the precise time at which the blood sample was taken from [Baby L], which was received in the lab at about 18.30 or thereabouts.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Taking midday as the earliest time at which it could have been taken, and 15.45 as the latest time, what effect would a delay in having taken it from the child, getting it to the lab to be spun and frozen -- what effect would that delay have on the readings for insulin and C-peptide? I think you deal with this in your report of 20 June.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So there's quite a reasonable data set on this area. I think the time frame that we are discussing and operating over is probably 6 hours, let's say. The data from MacDonald and Astley, my Lord, which I think I referenced and forwarded to the court, would argue for a 3% to 8% decline in the measured insulin if it had been delayed by 6 hours.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So the reading is a minimum reading rather than a maximum?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. If we are saying that the sample was taken at 12 o'clock and, for whatever reason, didn't get to the lab until 6 o'clock, then we could apply that argument to the value that was recorded so that instead of 1,099, the value would be higher than that.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: What about the C-peptide?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Equally. Equally so, yes. The 3% to 8% operates for both insulin and C-peptide in the MacDonald paper.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So does it have any effect on the ratio which, as I understand it at least, is the critical determinant of exogenous insulin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: None whatsoever.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: My Lord, it's bang on 1 o'clock or a minute short. I think that's probably the end, but can I just think about it?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Certainly. We'll break off there and if you have any more questions for the professor, you can ask them at 2 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So 2 o'clock then, please, members of the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
Thank you, professor. Ready to continue at 2 o'clock, please. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The matter that was raised at the end of yesterday, I have received the documents but I have not been able to view the relevant material yet. If we could wait until the end of today so far as evidence being placed before the jury is concerned and revisit that issue then.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'll see where we're up to and what time it is in relation to that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Has the download succeeded?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I've got the download, but I haven't had time to watch it yet. All right, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The short adjournment)
(In the presence of the jury)
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Professor Hindmarsh, could I just ask you a couple of points about the [Baby F] schedule that you created and which we
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: looked at, ladies and gentlemen, just towards the back of divider 6 in bundle 2. It's the schedule that you created, Professor Hindmarsh, so you may have it on your screen.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: We were looking at what lies behind or matters in relation to that figure of 2.9 at 05.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you see that, professor?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: When we received the table, dealing with 5 August, at the time of 01.54, we had a blood glucose reading of 0.8.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Then at 02.55 it was at 2.3.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Then at 04.02, it was down to 1.9.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And then 05.00, raised to 2.9, and at 08.09 back down to 1.7.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And then in the course of you giving evidence, I'd introduced the fact that in between the 0.8 and the 2.3 reading there had been a bolus of 10% dextrose at 02.05; do you recall that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I remember that discussion, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And in between 04.02 and 05.00, there'd been another -- I think it was a 10% bolus at 04.20.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And having reviewed this, I just want to confirm two matters with you, please, Professor Hindmarsh. They are to be taken together so let me put into of them to you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The first one is that the increase in dextrose from 0.8 at 01.54 to 2.3 at 02.55 reflects that 10% bolus that had been given?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think that's reasonable, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Against a background of ongoing insulin action. That's the thing that you would add to that; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's the premise on which I'd be working, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes. Likewise, between 04.02 and 05.00, the increase to 2.9 reflects the bolus at 04.20, but again against a background of ongoing insulin action?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Returning then to [Baby L], the first area I'm going to look at with your assistance, Professor Hindmarsh, is the period of hypoglycaemia with a particular view to where we can say with any certainty that exogenous insulin is or may have been introduced I just want everyone to follow where we are: we are looking at the overall period, where we can see what appears to be, from your analysis, insulin beyond what could be -hypoglycaemia beyond what could be naturally occurring.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: [Baby L] had neonatal hypoglycaemia from birth, didn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I'm going to be making reference to the table for [Baby L] that we've got. I'll just check we can all see that in front of you, ladies and gentlemen. You can see yours, Professor Hindmarsh?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So we know that at 12.00 hours on 8 April, a 10% -- a bag of 10% dextrose was put up. We can follow these timings on our table. We can see that in the hours that follow the 10% bag being put up, 12.14, it's at 2.5, so it's risen from the 1.9 earlier.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: 16.00 hours, 5.8, so that's risen significantly in the circumstances, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: 18.00, lower, but then the rate had already been reduced at that point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: When we look across, the dextrose had gone down to 1.6.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Going into that evening, we've got readings of 2.3 and 2.2 at 21.00 and 22.00 hours, haven't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, we have.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Which, as you said, subject to any enteral feeds, may reflect also the reduction in the rate of dextrose that he was receiving?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Then we have that reading at 24.00 hours of 3.6 for blood sugar. Again, that's consistent -- I'm going to suggest that's consistent potentially with ongoing infant hypoglycaemia at that point.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: 3.6 we would view as acceptable.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Right. So that's acceptable?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: As I understood it, the professor says 2.6 is the lowest limit, but some people say you can go down to 2.4.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So anything above 2.4 is within the acceptable range?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. I think -- precisely. Everyone would think if you'd gone up to 3.6, it's well above 3, so one could relax having seen that evolve.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you. So actually, then, if we look above the first black bar from 8 April to 9 April, although a couple of the readings later in the evening are perhaps just below the range we've just mentioned, taken as a body those are acceptable readings in the circumstances?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I think... Babies often become hypoglycaemic during the first 24 hours or have low blood glucose values as they adapt from the intrawomb environment to having to cope with an oral intake, which is variable in amount and in timing.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Right. So would you put it this way, Professor Hindmarsh, between 12.14 on 8 April through to about midnight, the readings are either in the normal range or consistent with what could otherwise be a transient neonatal hypoglycaemia?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. As I said, I'm happy with, firstly, the way they handled the situation and also in the likely explanation for the changes during that period of time.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Right. If we move forward now into 9 April, we have the reading at 10.00 of 1.9, which is, for these purposes, significantly below the acceptable level, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, indeed.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And that, if we're looking for a period from which we can say there is continuing hypoglycaemia that can't be explained by natural means, that would be where we can start from with any certainty on your analysis?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's my view, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So whatever has gone on either at 10.00 or in the period between midnight and 10.00 hours, something has happened to change that situation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Something has changed, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Something has changed. Then if we go forwards on your analysis, relying on the data you've been provided with, the period of non-natural hypoglycaemia, the period when, to get down to the issue, artificial insulin would be having an effect, is up to about 15.00 hours on 11 April, which is the last page of this table?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I think that's -- on what we have.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes, on what we have. So in terms of readings, we've got from 1.9 at 10 o'clock on 9 April to perhaps just before the 3.5 at 15.00 on 11 April. That's the period, the key period?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: With a question mark between midnight and 10.00 on 9 April as to when precisely this might have started?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think we just don't know.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: We just don't know.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The next thing I'd like your help with, Professor Hindmarsh, is just the blood glucose reading of 2.8 that we looked at. I'm sure you remember where it is, ladies and gentlemen, but for the sake of convenience, because it reflects when the sample arrived in the lab, it's on page 2 and it's slotted in around 18.26 to 18.29 hours on 9 April.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As you've heard, Professor Hindmarsh, it's in the table there because we have for sure the time that it arrives in the lab.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: In terms of the time at which the sample was taken, there's evidence to be considered on that, but it's, as you've heard, somewhere within the period either from 12 noon on the 9th to round about 15.45 on the 9th.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So can I just take us to that part of the table to put it in context. Ladies and gentlemen, if we, and you please, Professor Hindmarsh, go to the first page of the table. The sample is taken at some point during the period either from 12.00 hours when we can see there's a reading of 1.6; can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: To 15.45. Now we have a reading of 1.5 at 15.00 hours, don't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, between 15.00 hours and 16.00 hours, they're the same, so it's reasonable to assume it's 1.5.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And ladies and gentlemen, if you look -- you too, please, Professor Hindmarsh -- on page 2, 16.00 is 1.5, so it's bracketed by that reading, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you. You've explained that the plasma analysis will be about -- the finger prick will be about 10% to 15% less than the plasma analysis; that's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So although the glucose is 2.8, in fact that should reflect a finger prick figure of 2.4 or thereabouts?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thereabouts.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: As it happens, if we look at this, that's still, for whatever reason, way out from 1.6 or 1.5, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's different to those, yes, although bearing in mind there was a change in infusion rates.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes. But it's certainly -- the difference is significantly greater than what you would normally expect for there just being the 10% to 15% difference from a finger prick to plasma analysis, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: If that is applied across the readings we have, in fact they'd all be elevated from what we have on this table, wouldn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think we just need to err a little bit of caution in this, in that the 10% to 15% refers to the difference between plasma glucose and blood glucose in children and adults, and because we're also talking about -- the main difference, my Lord, I'm sorry about this, is because there's a water content of the red cells in the blood as opposed to plasma, which doesn't have any red cells.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: That's why you get this difference.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The number of red cells in neonates is slightly different to what you would -- you and I have. So that 10% to 15% may actually be higher than what we think.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So I'm not absolutely sure we can just take that and take it across the whole field. It's an extrapolation from adults and children.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: As it happens, though, looking at the front page of this table where you've got 12.00 and 15.40 and the readings of 1.6 and 1.5, going off the plasma reading it's still well above actually what they are, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We don't know what they are in corresponding to that.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The plasma, as we've just looked at, that occurs -- that specimen is taken at some point at or between 12.00 and 15.45, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we think that is correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: No, as a matter of evidence, we know it is across that time. That bit is clear, Professor Hindmarsh.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So as it happens, the readings, however it happens on the finger pricks, are well below what you would expect from applying your 10% to 15% to the plasma glucose, aren't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They are, but whatever way you look at it, they are all low.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Mm. Well, these are two of the lowest, aren't they, 1.6 and 1.5?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And they would come out on your 10% to 15% analysis as 2.4, wouldn't they, roughly?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not quite as high as that, but yes, okay.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Therefore if that applies across these readings, it'll be correspondingly higher on the other ones, won't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It could be, but as I say, whatever way you adjust it, they're still low and consistently low.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: 2.4 would be just on the edge of the normal range, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's what would be accepted in the first 24/48 hours of life in an infant who is well.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: But if 2.4 is the proper analysis reading for, let's say, 1.5 at 15.00 hours; can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Then if we go over the page, let's look at 18.00 hours where it says 1.9. Can you go to page 2? 18.00 hours on 9 April, you've got 1.9 just above the yellow bar.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: By the same factor, it's going to be significantly higher than 2.4, isn't it, a corrected blood glucose in that way. It is, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And it's going to take it into the acceptable range?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it might be acceptable on one occasion, but what we're seeing here is consistently low glucose concentrations. And as I said, the proviso on the interpretation of "Is it all right to have that kind of blood glucose value" is if you are a well baby.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I understand that. As in, I understand that's your explanation for that, Professor Hindmarsh.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I'm going to move to a different topic to do with administration of insulin if that is what has happened.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You've looked at with us ways in which insulin could have been administered to result in the readings that you have received from the analysis. In short, it would either be by a series of repeat injections or by infusion through the bag, the insulin having got there -- possibly having got there by one method or another?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Right. I know you nodded, you have to say yes or no.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I think we're probably all there with this, but the problem with different injections on multiple occasions is because Actrapid has such a fast action, there would have to be a lot of them going forwards if it was individual injections of insulin all the time or over the period?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: For that reason, your assessment is that it's more likely that insulin has been added, in one way or another, to a bag or bags of dextrose that were hung?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct. Perhaps in the -- in being fair, we should also consider the possibility that a long-acting insulin was used subcutaneously, but if we were going to go down that line -- because it would still need some multiple injections. But if we were going to pursue that line we would then have to
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: work out the source of that because long-acting insulin would not be conventional ward stock.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And the evidence is clear, there's no issue, that the insulin we're talking about is Actrapid in this case.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And dealing with the insulin that we're dealing with in the case, as you said, that would take upwards of seven or eight injections over a period of time to try and achieve this sort of effect?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I suggest that's probably at least, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, probably at least, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I think you explained on a previous occasion the halflife of this is about 20 to 25 minutes, with Actrapid, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. If it's given intravenously then the half-life of insulin is 4 minutes. Twenty to 25 minutes is the half-life of C-peptide --
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- which we've talked about, I think.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: All right. Let's look at the question of the infusion then. The period we are looking at, at the very least, if we're talking about insulin acting by way of the infusion, is from at least 10 o'clock on 9 April, which is the reading of 1.9, through to a period ending at or shortly before 15.00 hours on 11 April.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Right. Just going through the question of bags and how this would work, we know the first bag we're dealing with in this is hung at 12 o'clock on 8 April. So we can have a marker there. That's bag 1.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And on your assessment, Professor Hindmarsh, by the time we get to 10 o'clock on 9 April, something would have been added to that bag; is that correct? Insulin would have been added to that bag?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: That would have been added between midnight and 10 o'clock in the morning?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Assuming the bag wasn't changed.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And in fact, factoring in the half-life in the infusion, it would probably have to have been put in by 9.30 or thereabouts, wouldn't it, to have got to 1.9 at 10 o'clock?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right. As the latest time point.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: At the latest. It's some time between midnight and 9.30, right. Now, at 12.10, there's a question mark, we've seen, as to whether or not there is another bag there. That's 24 hours after the first one. We can put "question mark bag 2" because as a matter of evidence that's something to be considered.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: If a bag is put up at 12.10 and the giving set has changed, so I'm going to do it both ways, if the giving set has been changed then insulin would have to have been added to that new bag to carry on with the insulin values that we get?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: If we move forwards, the next bag change appears to be at 16.30 hours on 9 April, so that's over the page.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So that's bag 2 or bag 3 depending on how the evidence is on that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: If that bag is put up then and if the giving set was changed, again insulin would have to have been added to that new bag to maintain this at some point in some way?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Moving on, you identified for us, Professor Hindmarsh, on 10 April 2016 what appeared to you to be potentially a new bag. Is it between 10.30 and 3 in the morning, 02.30 and 03.00?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Only in the sense that you've got a change in the dextrose concentration.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Which in good practice would imply a change of bag.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'll take the point that we are talking about good practice here.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes. The point being, if we've been on a certain percentage -- on 12.5% dextrose up to then, for there to be a change to 15% between 02.30 and 3 o'clock, on the face of it, would be a change of bag because it's a different concentration of dextrose?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So that would be either bag 3 or bag 4. And if that is a bag change and if the giving set was changed, insulin would have to have been added to that bag to carry on with the blood glucose being depressed as it is?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: That's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: If we move forwards to 11 April, so towards the bottom of page 2, we can actually see at 01.45 it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Started by Caroline Oakley/Samantha O'Brien at a rate of 7.3ml per hour."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: That appears to be clearly a new bag that is hung at that time.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So that's bag 4 or bag 5 depending on where we are.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Again, if the giving set has been changed on that, then insulin would have to have been added to that new bag at some point to maintain the depression in the dextrose -- the blood sugar?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And then going over the page, that takes us to the period from about 15.00 when it seems, on your analysis, we come out of the questionable hypoglycaemia?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: All right. We've dealt there with the situation if insulin is added in the event of giving sets having been changed --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: -- whatever's happened on whichever occasion. If we're talking about the giving sets remaining the same or the giving set remaining the same, you've raised the possibility that given that insulin, as a protein, sticks to plastic, you could have, in effect, sticky insulin coming off --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: -- and continuing with the infusion?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I'm going to ask, surely that must run out at some point. There can't be an inexhaustible supply of sticky insulin over a period of about a day and a half running through this, can there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Right. Is it the case that sticky insulin could be operative over a certain period potentially?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think anybody's actually done those kind of studies, to be honest, and I think the answer is we simply don't know.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The hypoglycaemia that [Baby L] experiences over this period, is it in a relatively steady state, if you see what I mean? So the levels go up and down according to the dextrose that's being given?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, they do seem to be influenced by the infusion rates, and at different infusion rates, we do seem to achieve a relatively steady state.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes. If we're working with the question of insulin being added in some way or getting in there in some way, would that be more consistent with it being added to the bags as we go along
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: rather than an ever-diminishing supply of sticky insulin coming off the plastic?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. If you were just relying on the sticky insulin, you would have to probably come back a bit on your infusion rate because you would probably be overdoing it in parts.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes. So sticky insulin may account for some aspect of it, but over time it would really require additional insulin being required as we go along to maintain these levels?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is what I would view as correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you, Professor Hindmarsh.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR JOHNSON

Mr Myers prefaced a series of questions there with, "We're going to look at the administration of insulin, if that is what happened". Is there any question in these circumstances that that is what happened?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, you have information and pathology reports from 9 April in the analysis that I've provided on page 4, but it's also within the documents at J18026, which is the campatha(?) summary of the sample on that day, which clearly demonstrates the presence of insulin in a very high concentration of 1,099 picomoles per litre and a low plasma C-peptide concentration at 264 picomoles per litre. So I think we can be quite certain that at that time that exogenous insulin was present.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thereafter, despite a variety of background infusion rates of dextrose, there isn't really much change in the glucose measurements, which would imply that there is ongoing insulin present and ongoing insulin action.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: You told us this morning that a conservative estimate for the rate of circulation, and by that do I take it blood out of heart, blood back into heart, is 30 seconds in a neonate?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. That was when we were talking about achieving steady states, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes. So that's how long it takes --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: For the mixing.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: For the mixing, yes. Looking at the figure of 2.8, which is the blood sample taken some time between midday and 15.45, we see, looking at the bottom of page 1, that a bolus of 4.3ml 10% dextrose was given to [Baby L] at 15.40. If the blood
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON
